topics.title: Operators in Python
topics.content:
Arithmetic operators
  • + — addition
  • - — subtraction
  • * — multiplication
  • / — division (result is always a float)
  • // — integer division (discards the fractional part)
  • % — modulo (remainder of division)
  • ** — exponentiation

Examples:

print(10 / 3)   # 3.3333333333333335
print(10 // 3)  # 3
print(10 % 3)   # 1
print(2 ** 4)   # 16
Comparison operators
  • == — equal to
  • != — not equal to
  • < — less than
  • > — greater than
  • <= — less than or equal to
  • >= — greater than or equal to

The result is a Boolean value True or False.

Logical operators
  • and — logical AND (True if both operands are True)
  • or — logical OR (True if at least one operand is True)
  • not — logical NOT (inverts the value)
Assignment operators
  • = — simple assignment
  • +=, -=, *=, /= etc. — assignment with operation
x = 5
x += 3   # x = x + 3 → 8
Operator precedence

Arithmetic operators have the highest precedence, then comparisons, then logical operators. Parentheses () are used to explicitly specify the order of evaluation.

topics.title: Conditional statements: if, elif, else
topics.content:
Simple if
if condition:
    # code block executed if condition is true
if-else
if condition:
    # block 1
else:
    # block 2 (if condition is false)
if-elif-else
if condition1:
    # block 1
elif condition2:
    # block 2
else:
    # block 3 (if none of the conditions are true)

Example:

x = int(input())
if x > 0:
    print('Positive')
elif x == 0:
    print('Zero')
else:
    print('Negative')
Ternary operator

Short form of if-else:

value = a if condition else b

Example:

age = 20
status = 'adult' if age >= 18 else 'minor'

topics.title: The while loop
topics.content:
Syntax
while condition:
    # loop body

The loop runs as long as the condition is true. It is important to change variables that affect the condition to avoid an infinite loop.

Example
i = 0
while i < 5:
    print(i)
    i += 1
break

The break statement immediately terminates the loop.

i = 0
while True:
    print(i)
    i += 1
    if i >= 5:
        break
continue

The continue statement skips the rest of the loop body and moves to the next iteration.

i = 0
while i < 5:
    i += 1
    if i == 3:
        continue
    print(i)  # prints 1,2,4,5
else for while

The else block is executed if the loop terminates normally (not by break).

i = 0
while i < 3:
    print(i)
    i += 1
else:
    print('Loop finished')

topics.title: The for loop and the range() function
topics.content:
for syntax
for variable in sequence:
    # loop body

The loop iterates over all elements of a sequence (string, list, tuple, dictionary, set, etc.).

The range() function
  • range(stop) — numbers from 0 to stop-1
  • range(start, stop) — numbers from start to stop-1
  • range(start, stop, step) — numbers with step size

Examples:

for i in range(5):
    print(i)  # 0,1,2,3,4

for i in range(2, 8, 2):
    print(i)  # 2,4,6
Iterating over sequence elements
fruits = ['apple', 'banana', 'cherry']
for fruit in fruits:
    print(fruit)
Nested loops
for i in range(3):
    for j in range(2):
        print(i, j)
break and continue in for

Same as in the while loop.

topics.title: String methods
topics.content:
All string methods return a new string because strings are immutable.

Changing case
s = 'Hello World'
print(s.upper())      # 'HELLO WORLD'
print(s.lower())      # 'hello world'
print(s.capitalize()) # 'Hello world'
print(s.title())      # 'Hello World'
Removing whitespace
s = '  Hello  '
print(s.strip())   # 'Hello' (removes leading and trailing spaces)
print(s.lstrip())  # 'Hello  ' (left)
print(s.rstrip())  # '  Hello' (right)
Search and replace
s = 'Hello World'
print(s.find('World'))    # 6 (starting index)
print(s.find('Python'))   # -1
print(s.replace('World', 'Python'))  # 'Hello Python'
Split and join
s = 'a,b,c'
lst = s.split(',')        # ['a', 'b', 'c']
new_s = '-'.join(lst)     # 'a-b-c'
Checks
'123'.isdigit()    # True
'abc'.isalpha()    # True
'ab12'.isalnum()   # True
'   '.isspace()    # True
'Hello'.startswith('He') # True
'World'.endswith('ld')   # True

topics.title: String formatting
topics.content:
Old style (% operator)
name = 'Alice'
age = 25
print('My name is %s, I am %d years old.' % (name, age))
The format() method
print('My name is {}, I am {} years old.'.format(name, age))
print('My name is {1}, I am {0} years old.'.format(age, name))  # with indices
print('My name is {name}, I am {age} years old.'.format(name='Alice', age=25))
f-strings (Python 3.6+) — recommended way
print(f'My name is {name}, I am {age} years old.')
# can use expressions
print(f'In 5 years I will be {age + 5} years old.')

# number formatting
pi = 3.1415926
print(f'{pi:.2f}')  # '3.14'

topics.title: Lists: creation and basic operations
topics.content:
Creating a list
lst1 = [1, 2, 3]
lst2 = list('abc')      # ['a', 'b', 'c']
lst3 = []               # empty list
Indexing and slicing

Same as strings:

lst = [10, 20, 30, 40]
print(lst[0])    # 10
print(lst[-1])   # 40
print(lst[1:3])  # [20, 30]
Modifying elements
lst[0] = 99
print(lst)       # [99, 20, 30, 40]
Adding elements
lst.append(50)   # adds to the end
print(lst)       # [99,20,30,40,50]
lst.insert(1, 15)# inserts at index 1
print(lst)       # [99,15,20,30,40,50]
Removing elements
del lst[2]       # deletes element by index
x = lst.pop()    # removes and returns the last element
y = lst.pop(0)   # removes and returns element at index 0
lst.remove(30)   # removes the first occurrence of value 30
Clearing and copying
lst.clear()
lst_copy = lst.copy()   # shallow copy

topics.title: List methods and operations
topics.content:
extend()

Adds elements of another list (or any iterable) to the end.

a = [1,2]
a.extend([3,4])
print(a)  # [1,2,3,4]
index() and count()
lst = [1,2,3,2,1]
print(lst.index(2))   # 1 (first occurrence)
print(lst.count(2))   # 2
sort() and reverse()
lst = [3,1,4,1,5]
lst.sort()            # sorts the list in place
print(lst)            # [1,1,3,4,5]
lst.reverse()         # reverses the list
print(lst)            # [5,4,3,1,1]
Functions for working with lists
lst = [3,1,4,1,5]
print(len(lst))       # 5
print(min(lst))       # 1
print(max(lst))       # 5
print(sum(lst))       # 14
Sorting that creates a new list
new_lst = sorted(lst)   # does not modify the original
Copying (full and partial)
a = [1,2,3]
b = a[:]                 # copy via slice
c = a.copy()             # same

topics.title: List comprehensions
topics.content:
Basic syntax
[expression for variable in sequence if condition]
Examples
# squares of numbers from 0 to 9
squares = [x**2 for x in range(10)]
print(squares)  # [0,1,4,9,16,25,36,49,64,81]

# only even numbers
evens = [x for x in range(10) if x % 2 == 0]
print(evens)    # [0,2,4,6,8]

# combination of two loops
pairs = [(x,y) for x in range(3) for y in range(2)]
print(pairs)    # [(0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1),(2,0),(2,1)]
Analogues for sets and dictionaries
# set
s = {x**2 for x in range(5)}  # {0,1,4,9,16}

# dictionary
d = {x: x**2 for x in range(5)}  # {0:0,1:1,2:4,3:9,4:16}

topics.title: Tuples
topics.content:
Creating a tuple
t1 = (1, 2, 3)
t2 = 1, 2, 3      # without parentheses (packing)
t3 = (5,)          # single‑element tuple (comma is required)
Immutability

Tuple elements cannot be changed after creation. Trying to assign a value will raise an error.

Indexing and slicing

Same as for lists.

Tuple methods
t = (1,2,3,2,1)
print(t.count(2))   # 2
print(t.index(3))   # 2
Tuple unpacking
point = (10, 20)
x, y = point        # x=10, y=20

# can use * to capture the remaining elements
a, *b, c = (1,2,3,4,5)   # a=1, b=[2,3,4], c=5
Advantages of tuples
  • Take less memory than lists.
  • Can be used as dictionary keys (because they are immutable).
  • Often used to return multiple values from a function.

topics.title: Dictionaries: creation and access
topics.content:
Creating a dictionary
d1 = {'key1': 'value1', 'key2': 'value2'}
d2 = dict(key1='value1', key2='value2')  # keys as strings
d3 = {}            # empty dictionary
Access by key
print(d1['key1'])  # 'value1'
# if the key does not exist, KeyError is raised
# safe access:
print(d1.get('key3', 'default'))   # 'default'
Adding and modifying
d1['new_key'] = 'new_value'   # adds a new key‑value pair
d1['key1'] = 'new'            # modifies an existing one
Deleting
del d1['key1']
value = d1.pop('key2')        # removes and returns the value
Checking for key existence
if 'key1' in d1:
    print('exists')
Length of dictionary
len(d1)

topics.title: Dictionary methods and iteration
topics.content:
keys(), values(), items() methods
d = {'a':1, 'b':2, 'c':3}
print(d.keys())    # dict_keys(['a','b','c'])
print(d.values())  # dict_values([1,2,3])
print(d.items())   # dict_items([('a',1),('b',2),('c',3)])
Iterating over a dictionary
for key in d:
    print(key, d[key])

for key, value in d.items():
    print(key, value)
Updating a dictionary
d.update({'d':4, 'e':5})   # adds pairs or updates existing ones
Copying
d_copy = d.copy()   # shallow copy
Clearing
d.clear()
Sorting keys
sorted(d)   # returns a list of sorted keys

topics.title: Sets and frozenset
topics.content:
Creating a set
s1 = {1, 2, 3}
s2 = set([1,2,3,2])   # {1,2,3}
s3 = set()            # empty set (not {}, that is a dictionary)
Operations on elements
s = {1,2,3}
s.add(4)              # {1,2,3,4}
s.remove(2)           # removes 2; if not present, raises error
s.discard(5)          # removes if present; no error if missing
x = s.pop()           # removes and returns an arbitrary element
Set operations
a = {1,2,3}
b = {3,4,5}
print(a.union(b))           # {1,2,3,4,5}  (a | b)
print(a.intersection(b))    # {3}          (a & b)
print(a.difference(b))      # {1,2}        (a - b)
print(a.symmetric_difference(b)) # {1,2,4,5} (a ^ b)
Checks
print(2 in a)          # True
print(a.issubset(b))   # False
print(a.issuperset(b)) # False
frozenset

An immutable set, can be used as a dictionary key.

fs = frozenset([1,2,3])

topics.title: Functions: definition and call
topics.content:
Function definition
def name(parameters):
    '''documentation (docstring)'''
    body
    return value
Example
def greet(name):
    '''Returns a greeting'''
    return f'Hello, {name}!'

print(greet('Alice'))   # 'Hello, Alice!'
Parameters

Parameters can be mandatory or optional (with default values).

def power(x, n=2):
    return x ** n

print(power(3))    # 9 (n defaults to 2)
print(power(3,3))  # 27
Return value

If return is omitted or used without an argument, the function returns None.

Documentation
def my_func():
    '''This is documentation.'''
    pass

help(my_func)   # displays the documentation

topics.title: Function arguments: positional and keyword
topics.content:
Positional arguments

Passed in the order defined by the function.

def func(a, b, c):
    print(a,b,c)

func(1,2,3)   # 1 2 3
Keyword (named) arguments

Passed with the name of the parameter. Order does not matter.

func(c=3, a=1, b=2)   # 1 2 3
Combination

Positional arguments come first, then keyword arguments.

func(1, c=3, b=2)     # 1 2 3
Default values

Parameters with default values must follow mandatory ones.

def func(a, b=10, c=20):
    print(a,b,c)

func(1)        # 1 10 20
func(1,5)      # 1 5 20
func(1, c=30)  # 1 10 30

topics.title: Arbitrary number of arguments: *args and **kwargs
topics.content:
*args — arbitrary number of positional arguments

All passed arguments are collected into a tuple.

def func(*args):
    for arg in args:
        print(arg)

func(1,2,3,4)   # 1 2 3 4
**kwargs — arbitrary number of keyword arguments

Arguments are collected into a dictionary.

def func(**kwargs):
    for key, value in kwargs.items():
        print(key, value)

func(a=1, b=2, c=3)   # a 1, b 2, c 3
Using together
def func(required, *args, **kwargs):
    print(required)
    print(args)
    print(kwargs)

func(1, 2,3,4, x=5, y=6)
# 1
# (2,3,4)
# {'x':5, 'y':6}

The names args and kwargs are not mandatory, but they are conventional.

topics.title: Variable scope
topics.content:
Local variables

Variables defined inside a function are accessible only within that function.

def func():
    x = 10   # local
    print(x)

func()
# print(x)  # error
Global variables

Variables defined outside functions are accessible throughout the code. Inside a function, they can be read, but to modify them we need the global keyword.

x = 5
def func():
    global x
    x = 10

func()
print(x)   # 10
nonlocal

Used in nested functions to modify a variable from the outer (but not global) scope.

def outer():
    x = 1
    def inner():
        nonlocal x
        x = 2
    inner()
    print(x)   # 2
Built‑in functions locals() and globals()

Return dictionaries of local and global variables, respectively.

topics.title: Lambda functions
topics.content:
Syntax
lambda parameters: expression

A lambda function is an anonymous function that returns the result of evaluating the expression.

Examples
square = lambda x: x**2
print(square(5))   # 25

# use with map
numbers = [1,2,3,4]
squared = list(map(lambda x: x**2, numbers))
print(squared)     # [1,4,9,16]

# use with filter
evens = list(filter(lambda x: x % 2 == 0, numbers))
print(evens)       # [2,4]

# sorting by key
pairs = [(1, 'one'), (3, 'three'), (2, 'two')]
pairs.sort(key=lambda pair: pair[0])
print(pairs)       # [(1,'one'),(2,'two'),(3,'three')]
Limitations

A lambda cannot contain statements, only a single expression.

topics.title: Recursion
topics.content:
Definition

Recursion is when a function calls itself. There must be a base case (exit condition), otherwise the function will call itself indefinitely.

Example: factorial
def factorial(n):
    if n <= 1:
        return 1
    else:
        return n * factorial(n-1)

print(factorial(5))   # 120
Example: Fibonacci numbers
def fib(n):
    if n <= 1:
        return n
    else:
        return fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)

print(fib(10))   # 55
Memoisation (caching results)

To speed up recursive functions, you can use the lru_cache decorator from functools.

from functools import lru_cache

@lru_cache(maxsize=None)
def fib(n):
    if n <= 1:
        return n
    return fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)
Recursion depth

By default, the recursion depth limit in Python is about 1000. You can change it with sys.setrecursionlimit(new_limit).

topics.title: Exception handling: try, except, finally
topics.content:
Exceptions

Exceptions occur at runtime due to errors (division by zero, accessing a non‑existent key, invalid input, etc.).

try‑except block
try:
    x = int(input('Enter a number: '))
except ValueError:
    print('That is not a number')
Multiple except
try:
    # code
except ValueError:
    # handle ValueError
except ZeroDivisionError:
    # handle division by zero
else block

Executed if no exception occurred.

try:
    x = int(input())
except ValueError:
    print('Error')
else:
    print(f'You entered {x}')
finally block

Executed always, regardless of whether an exception occurred or not. Used for closing files, releasing resources.

f = None
try:
    f = open('file.txt')
    # work with file
except FileNotFoundError:
    print('File not found')
finally:
    if f:
        f.close()
Catching any exception
try:
    # code
except Exception as e:
    print(f'Error: {e}')

topics.title: Custom exceptions and raise
topics.content:
Raising exceptions
raise ValueError('Invalid value')
Creating custom exceptions

Create a class that inherits from Exception (or a subclass of it).

class MyError(Exception):
    pass

def check_value(x):
    if x < 0:
        raise MyError('Negative number is not allowed')

try:
    check_value(-5)
except MyError as e:
    print(f'Error: {e}')
Re‑raising an exception

Use raise without arguments inside an except block to re‑raise the caught exception.

try:
    # code
except ValueError:
    print('Handling')
    raise   # the exception will be raised again

topics.title: File handling: reading and writing
topics.content:
Opening a file
file = open('filename.txt', 'mode')

Modes:

  • 'r' — read (default)
  • 'w' — write (creates a new file or overwrites)
  • 'a' — append to the end
  • 'rb' — read in binary mode
  • 'wb' — write in binary mode
Reading from a file
with open('file.txt', 'r', encoding='utf-8') as f:
    content = f.read()         # whole file as a single string
    lines = f.readlines()       # list of lines
    for line in f:              # iterate over lines
        print(line)
Writing to a file
with open('file.txt', 'w', encoding='utf-8') as f:
    f.write('Hello, world!\n')
    f.writelines(['line1\n', 'line2\n'])
The with block

Guarantees that the file is closed even if an error occurs. Recommended to use always.

Working with CSV
import csv

# reading
with open('data.csv') as f:
    reader = csv.reader(f)
    for row in reader:
        print(row)

# writing
with open('data.csv', 'w') as f:
    writer = csv.writer(f)
    writer.writerow(['Name', 'Age'])
    writer.writerow(['Alice', 25])

topics.title: Modules and imports
topics.content:
What is a module?

A module is a file with a .py extension that contains functions, variables, and classes. Modules allow code organisation and reuse.

Importing a module
import math                # imports the whole module
print(math.sqrt(16))       # 4.0

from math import sqrt, pi  # imports specific functions
print(sqrt(25))            # 5.0

import math as m           # import with an alias
print(m.cos(0))            # 1.0
Module search path

The interpreter looks for modules in the list of paths sys.path (current directory, installed packages).

Packages

A package is a folder containing modules and a (possibly empty) __init__.py file. It allows organising modules hierarchically.

import mypackage.mymodule
from mypackage import mymodule
Preventing execution on import
if __name__ == '__main__':
    # code will run only when the file is executed as a script
    main()

topics.title: Standard library: math module
topics.content:
Constants
import math
print(math.pi)   # 3.141592653589793
print(math.e)    # 2.718281828459045
print(math.inf)  # infinity
print(math.nan)  # not a number
Main functions
  • math.sqrt(x) — square root
  • math.pow(x, y) — x to the power y
  • math.exp(x) — e^x
  • math.log(x, base) — logarithm with given base (default e)
  • math.log10(x) — base‑10 logarithm
  • math.sin(x), math.cos(x), math.tan(x) — trigonometric functions (x in radians)
  • math.asin(x), math.acos(x), math.atan(x) — inverse trigonometric
  • math.degrees(x) — convert radians to degrees
  • math.radians(x) — convert degrees to radians
  • math.factorial(x) — factorial
  • math.gcd(a,b) — greatest common divisor
  • math.ceil(x) — round up
  • math.floor(x) — round down
  • math.trunc(x) — discard the fractional part

topics.title: Standard library: random module
topics.content:
Main functions
  • random.random() — random float in [0.0, 1.0)
  • random.randint(a, b) — random integer from a to b inclusive
  • random.uniform(a, b) — random float in [a, b]
  • random.choice(seq) — random element from a sequence
  • random.shuffle(lst) — shuffles the list in place
  • random.sample(population, k) — sample of k unique elements
Examples
import random

print(random.random())
print(random.randint(1,10))
print(random.choice(['red','green','blue']))

deck = list(range(52))
random.shuffle(deck)
print(deck[:5])
Seed

For reproducibility, you can set a seed.

random.seed(42)
print(random.randint(1,10))  # will always produce the same result with the same seed

topics.title: Standard library: datetime module
topics.content:
Classes
  • datetime.date — date (year, month, day)
  • datetime.time — time (hour, minute, second, microsecond)
  • datetime.datetime — date + time
  • datetime.timedelta — difference between times/dates
Creating objects
from datetime import date, time, datetime, timedelta

d = date(2023, 12, 31)
t = time(23, 59, 30)
dt = datetime(2023, 12, 31, 23, 59, 30)

print(date.today())         # today's date
print(datetime.now())       # current date and time
Formatting and parsing
# date -> string
print(dt.strftime('%d.%m.%Y %H:%M'))   # '31.12.2023 23:59'

# string -> date
dt2 = datetime.strptime('31.12.2023 23:59', '%d.%m.%Y %H:%M')
Arithmetic
delta = timedelta(days=5, hours=3)
new_dt = dt + delta
print(new_dt)

difference = dt2 - dt   # timedelta

topics.title: Standard library: os and sys modules
topics.content:
os module

Provides functions for interacting with the operating system.

import os

print(os.getcwd())          # current directory
print(os.listdir('.'))      # list of files in the folder
os.mkdir('new_folder')      # create a folder
os.remove('file.txt')       # delete a file
os.path.join('folder', 'file.txt')  # join paths
os.path.exists('file.txt')  # check if file exists
sys module

Access to system parameters and functions.

import sys

print(sys.argv)            # command‑line arguments
sys.exit(0)                # terminate the program
print(sys.version)         # Python version
print(sys.path)            # module search paths

topics.title: Object‑oriented programming (OOP) basics
topics.content:
Classes and objects

A class is a template for creating objects. An object is a concrete instance of a class, with its own data (attributes) and behaviour (methods).

Defining a class
class Dog:
    def __init__(self, name, age):
        self.name = name   # instance attribute
        self.age = age

    def bark(self):        # method
        print(f'{self.name} says Woof!')

my_dog = Dog('Buddy', 3)
print(my_dog.name)   # 'Buddy'
my_dog.bark()        # 'Buddy says Woof!'
The __init__ method

The constructor, called when an object is created. The first parameter is self, a reference to the object itself.

Class attributes and instance attributes
class Dog:
    species = 'Canis familiaris'   # class attribute (shared by all)

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name           # instance attribute

topics.title: Inheritance and polymorphism
topics.content:
Inheritance

Allows creating a new class based on an existing (parent) class. The child class inherits all attributes and methods of the parent.

class Animal:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
    def speak(self):
        pass

class Dog(Animal):
    def speak(self):
        return f'{self.name} says Woof!'

class Cat(Animal):
    def speak(self):
        return f'{self.name} says Meow!'

animals = [Dog('Buddy'), Cat('Kitty')]
for animal in animals:
    print(animal.speak())   # polymorphism
Method overriding

The child class can provide its own version of a parent method.

super()

Calls the parent class method.

class Dog(Animal):
    def __init__(self, name, breed):
        super().__init__(name)   # call parent constructor
        self.breed = breed

topics.title: Encapsulation and the @property decorator
topics.content:
Encapsulation

Hiding internal data of an object. In Python there are no strict access modifiers, but there are conventions:

  • _name — protected attribute (not recommended to access directly).
  • __name — private attribute (name is mangled, access outside the class is difficult).
@property decorator

Allows defining methods for reading, modifying, and deleting an attribute while preserving attribute‑like access syntax.

class Person:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self._name = name

    @property
    def name(self):
        return self._name

    @name.setter
    def name(self, value):
        if not value:
            raise ValueError('Name cannot be empty')
        self._name = value

p = Person('Alice')
print(p.name)   # 'Alice'
p.name = 'Bob'
print(p.name)   # 'Bob'

topics.title: Magic methods (dunder methods)
topics.content:
What are magic methods?

Methods with double underscores at the beginning and end, defining object behaviour in standard situations (e.g., addition, conversion to string, etc.).

Common magic methods
  • __init__(self, ...) — constructor
  • __str__(self) — called when converting to string (print, str)
  • __repr__(self) — for debugging, should give a complete representation
  • __len__(self) — called by len()
  • __getitem__(self, key) — for index access (obj[key])
  • __setitem__(self, key, value) — assignment by index
  • __delitem__(self, key) — deletion by index
  • __contains__(self, item) — for the in operator
  • __call__(self, ...) — allows the object to be called as a function
  • __eq__(self, other), __lt__(self, other) — for comparisons
Example
class Point:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y
    def __str__(self):
        return f'({self.x},{self.y})'
    def __add__(self, other):
        return Point(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y)

p1 = Point(1,2)
p2 = Point(3,4)
print(p1 + p2)   # (4,6)

topics.title: Iterators and generators
topics.content:
Iterators

An object that implements the __iter__() method (returns itself) and the __next__() method (returns the next element). When elements are exhausted, __next__() must raise a StopIteration exception.

class Counter:
    def __init__(self, limit):
        self.limit = limit
        self.value = 0
    def __iter__(self):
        return self
    def __next__(self):
        if self.value >= self.limit:
            raise StopIteration
        self.value += 1
        return self.value

for i in Counter(5):
    print(i)   # 1 2 3 4 5
Generators

Functions that use yield instead of return. When called, they return a generator object, which is an iterator.

def count_up_to(limit):
    i = 1
    while i <= limit:
        yield i
        i += 1

for num in count_up_to(5):
    print(num)
Generator expressions
squares = (x**2 for x in range(10))
print(next(squares))   # 0
print(list(squares))   # the remaining ones

topics.title: Function decorators
topics.content:
What is a decorator?

A decorator is a function that takes another function and returns a new one, extending its behaviour without modifying the original code.

Simple decorator
def timer(func):
    import time
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        start = time.time()
        result = func(*args, **kwargs)
        end = time.time()
        print(f'Execution time: {end-start:.4f} sec')
        return result
    return wrapper

@timer
def slow_func():
    time.sleep(2)

slow_func()
Decorators with arguments
def repeat(n):
    def decorator(func):
        def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
            for _ in range(n):
                func(*args, **kwargs)
        return wrapper
    return decorator

@repeat(3)
def say_hi():
    print('Hi')

say_hi()   # 'Hi' 'Hi' 'Hi'

topics.title: Regular expressions (re module)
topics.content:
Main functions
  • re.search(pattern, string) — finds the first match, returns a Match object or None
  • re.match(pattern, string) — searches only at the beginning of the string
  • re.findall(pattern, string) — returns a list of all matches
  • re.finditer(pattern, string) — iterator of Match objects
  • re.sub(pattern, repl, string) — replaces all matches
  • re.split(pattern, string) — splits the string by the pattern
Regex syntax
  • . — any character
  • ^ — start of string
  • $ — end of string
  • * — 0 or more repetitions
  • + — 1 or more
  • ? — 0 or 1
  • {n,m} — from n to m repetitions
  • [abc] — any of the characters a, b, c
  • [^abc] — any character except a, b, c
  • \d — digit
  • \D — non‑digit
  • \w — letter, digit or underscore
  • \W — not a letter, digit or underscore
  • \s — whitespace character
  • \S — non‑whitespace
  • | — or
  • () — group
Examples
import re

text = 'My email is test@example.com'
result = re.search(r'\S+@\S+\.\S+', text)
if result:
    print(result.group())   # test@example.com

# findall
print(re.findall(r'\d+', 'a123b45c'))  # ['123', '45']

# sub
print(re.sub(r'\s+', '-', 'Hello   world'))  # 'Hello-world'

topics.title: Working with JSON
topics.content:
What is JSON?

JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a text‑based data exchange format based on JavaScript syntax. Widely used for data transfer between server and client.

The json module
  • json.dumps(obj) — converts a Python object to a JSON string
  • json.loads(s) — converts a JSON string to a Python object
  • json.dump(obj, file) — writes an object to a file in JSON format
  • json.load(file) — reads a JSON object from a file
Examples
import json

data = {
    'name': 'Alice',
    'age': 25,
    'courses': ['Math', 'Physics']
}

# Python -> JSON string
json_str = json.dumps(data, ensure_ascii=False, indent=4)
print(json_str)

# JSON string -> Python
restored = json.loads(json_str)
print(restored['name'])

# Write to file
with open('data.json', 'w', encoding='utf-8') as f:
    json.dump(data, f, ensure_ascii=False, indent=4)

# Read from file
with open('data.json', 'r', encoding='utf-8') as f:
    data_from_file = json.load(f)

topics.title: Introduction to NumPy
topics.content:
What is NumPy?

NumPy (Numerical Python) is a library for scientific computing. It provides multidimensional arrays and efficient functions to process them.

Installation
pip install numpy
Creating arrays
import numpy as np

a = np.array([1,2,3])            # 1‑dimensional array
b = np.array([[1,2], [3,4]])     # 2‑dimensional (matrix)

zeros = np.zeros((2,3))          # array of zeros
ones = np.ones((2,3))            # array of ones
empty = np.empty((2,3))          # uninitialised array

arange = np.arange(10)           # [0,1,2,...,9]
linspace = np.linspace(0,1,5)    # 5 evenly spaced numbers from 0 to 1
Basic operations
a = np.array([1,2,3])
b = np.array([4,5,6])
print(a + b)      # [5 7 9]
print(a * 2)      # [2 4 6]
print(np.sqrt(a)) # [1. 1.41421356 1.73205081]

# sum, mean, min, max
print(np.sum(a), np.mean(a), np.min(a), np.max(a))
Indexing and slicing
arr = np.array([[1,2,3],[4,5,6]])
print(arr[0,1])          # 2
print(arr[:,1])          # [2 5] (second column)

topics.title: Introduction to Pandas
topics.content:
What is Pandas?

Pandas is a data analysis library that provides DataFrame (tables) and Series (1‑dimensional arrays) data structures.

Installation
pip install pandas
Creating a DataFrame
import pandas as pd

data = {
    'Name': ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Charlie'],
    'Age': [25, 30, 35],
    'City': ['Moscow', 'London', 'New York']
}
df = pd.DataFrame(data)
print(df)
Reading / writing CSV
df = pd.read_csv('file.csv')
df.to_csv('out.csv', index=False)
Basic methods
print(df.head())          # first 5 rows
print(df.info())          # information about the data
print(df.describe())      # statistics

print(df['Name'])         # column 'Name'
print(df.loc[0])          # row with index 0
print(df.iloc[0,1])       # value at first row, second column

# grouping
grouped = df.groupby('City').mean()
print(grouped)
Handling missing values
df.dropna()          # remove rows with NaN
df.fillna(0)         # replace NaN with 0

topics.title: Testing code: assert and unittest
topics.content:
assert statements

assert checks a condition; if it is false, an AssertionError is raised.

def add(a,b):
    return a + b

assert add(2,2) == 4
assert add(2,-2) == 0
# if any assertion fails, the program stops with an error
The unittest module

Allows writing and running automated tests.

import unittest

def add(a,b):
    return a + b

class TestAdd(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_add_positive(self):
        self.assertEqual(add(2,3), 5)
    def test_add_negative(self):
        self.assertEqual(add(-1,-1), -2)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    unittest.main()

Main assert methods:

  • assertEqual(a,b) — a == b
  • assertTrue(x) — x is True
  • assertFalse(x) — x is False
  • assertRaises(exception, callable, *args, **kwargs) — checks that an exception is raised

topics.title: Virtual environments and pip
topics.content:
Why virtual environments?

They isolate project dependencies: libraries installed in one project do not affect another. This prevents version conflicts.

Creating a virtual environment
python -m venv myenv
Activation
  • Windows: myenv\Scripts\activate
  • macOS/Linux: source myenv/bin/activate

After activation, the command prompt shows the prefix (myenv).

Deactivating
deactivate
The pip package manager
pip install package_name   # install a package
pip list                   # list installed packages
pip freeze > requirements.txt   # save dependencies to a file
pip install -r requirements.txt # install all dependencies from a file

topics.title: PEP 8: coding style
topics.content:
What is PEP 8?

PEP 8 is the official style guide for writing Python code. Following these rules makes code more readable and consistent.

Basic rules
  • Indentation: 4 spaces (no tabs).
  • Maximum line length: 79 characters (72 for docstrings).
  • Blank lines: two blank lines between functions and classes, one between methods.
  • Whitespace: around binary operators (=, +, -, etc.), but not around default argument assignments.
  • Naming:
    • variables and functions — snake_case
    • classes — CamelCase
    • constants — ALL_CAPS
  • Imports: one import per line, first standard library, then third‑party, then local modules.
Style checkers

You can use linters such as flake8 or pylint.

topics.title: Type hints
topics.content:
What are type hints?

Type hints are a syntactic way to indicate the expected types of variables, arguments, and return values. They do not affect execution but help IDEs and static analysers (e.g., mypy) to find errors.

Syntax
def greet(name: str) -> str:
    return f'Hello, {name}'

age: int = 25
The typing module

For complex types:

from typing import List, Tuple, Dict, Optional, Union

# list of integers
def process(nums: List[int]) -> int:
    return sum(nums)

# tuple of a string and an integer
def get_info() -> Tuple[str, int]:
    return ('Alice', 25)

# dictionary with string keys and integer values
def get_counts() -> Dict[str, int]:
    return {'a':1, 'b':2}

# parameter may be int or None (Optional[int] is the same as Union[int, None])
def square(x: Optional[int]) -> int:
    if x is None:
        return 0
    return x * x

topics.title: Working with dates and times: the time module
topics.content:
Main functions
  • time.time() — seconds since 1 January 1970 (epoch).
  • time.sleep(sec) — suspends execution for the given number of seconds.
  • time.localtime([sec]) — converts time to a struct_time structure (year, month, day, hour, minute, second, etc.).
  • time.strftime(format, tm) — formats a time structure into a string.
  • time.strptime(string, format) — parses a string into a time structure.
Examples
import time

print(time.time())                # 1681234567.89

time.sleep(2)                     # pause 2 seconds

now = time.localtime()
print(now.tm_year, now.tm_mon)

formatted = time.strftime('%d.%m.%Y %H:%M', now)
print(formatted)                   # '31.12.2023 23:59'

parsed = time.strptime('31.12.2023 23:59', '%d.%m.%Y %H:%M')
print(parsed)
Difference between time and datetime

datetime is more convenient for calendar dates, time is for low‑level time operations and delays.

topics.title: Context managers and the with statement
topics.content:
What is a context manager?

A context manager is an object that defines methods __enter__ and __exit__, allowing it to be used in a with block. This is convenient for managing resources (files, connections), guaranteeing they are released after the block finishes.

Creating your own context manager
class ManagedFile:
    def __init__(self, filename):
        self.filename = filename
    def __enter__(self):
        self.file = open(self.filename, 'w')
        return self.file
    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, exc_tb):
        if self.file:
            self.file.close()

with ManagedFile('test.txt') as f:
    f.write('Hello, world!')
Using contextlib

The contextlib module simplifies creating context managers.

from contextlib import contextmanager

@contextmanager
def managed_file(filename):
    try:
        f = open(filename, 'w')
        yield f
    finally:
        f.close()

with managed_file('test.txt') as f:
    f.write('Hello, world!')
